title: How do customers rate their orders?
why: Start with the baseline: the spread of review scores.
sql:
SELECT score,
       COUNT(*) AS reviews,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 1) AS pct
FROM reviews
GROUP BY score
ORDER BY score;

title: Does delivery decide the rating?
why: Split reviewed orders by whether they arrived by the promised date.
sql:
SELECT CASE
         WHEN o.delivered_at IS NULL THEN 'Not delivered'
         WHEN o.delivered_at > o.estimated_at THEN 'Late'
         ELSE 'On time'
       END AS delivery,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       ROUND(AVG(r.score), 2) AS avg_score,
       ROUND(100.0 * AVG(r.score <= 2), 1) AS pct_bad
FROM orders o
JOIN reviews r USING (order_id)
GROUP BY delivery
ORDER BY avg_score DESC;

title: How much of the bad feeling comes from delivery?
why: Share of all 1 and 2 star reviews, against share of orders.
sql:
WITH d AS (
  SELECT CASE
           WHEN o.delivered_at IS NULL THEN 'Not delivered'
           WHEN o.delivered_at > o.estimated_at THEN 'Late'
           ELSE 'On time'
         END AS delivery,
         COUNT(*) AS orders,
         SUM(r.score <= 2) AS bad
  FROM orders o JOIN reviews r USING (order_id)
  GROUP BY delivery
)
SELECT delivery, orders, bad,
       ROUND(100.0 * orders / SUM(orders) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_orders,
       ROUND(100.0 * bad / SUM(bad) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_bad
FROM d
ORDER BY pct_of_bad DESC;

title: Does arriving very early earn better reviews?
why: Deliveries grouped by how far they landed from the promised date.
sql:
WITH d AS (
  SELECT julianday(o.delivered_at) - julianday(o.estimated_at) AS days, r.score
  FROM orders o JOIN reviews r USING (order_id)
  WHERE o.delivered_at IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT CASE
         WHEN days <= -21 THEN '1. 3+ weeks early'
         WHEN days <= -14 THEN '2. 2 to 3 weeks early'
         WHEN days <= -7  THEN '3. 1 to 2 weeks early'
         WHEN days <= 0   THEN '4. Up to 1 week early'
         WHEN days <= 7   THEN '5. Up to 1 week late'
         ELSE '6. Over 1 week late'
       END AS vs_promise,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       ROUND(AVG(score), 2) AS avg_score
FROM d
GROUP BY vs_promise
ORDER BY vs_promise;

title: How padded are the delivery promises?
why: Average promised days against actual days, for delivered orders.
sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS delivered_orders,
       ROUND(AVG(julianday(estimated_at) - julianday(purchased_at)), 1) AS promised_days,
       ROUND(AVG(julianday(delivered_at) - julianday(purchased_at)), 1) AS actual_days,
       ROUND(AVG(julianday(estimated_at) - julianday(delivered_at)), 1) AS days_early,
       ROUND(100.0 * AVG(delivered_at > estimated_at), 1) AS pct_late
FROM orders
WHERE delivered_at IS NOT NULL;

title: Where are promises broken most?
why: Late rate by customer state, for states with at least 500 delivered orders.
sql:
SELECT state,
       COUNT(*) AS delivered_orders,
       ROUND(100.0 * AVG(delivered_at > estimated_at), 1) AS pct_late,
       ROUND(AVG(julianday(estimated_at) - julianday(delivered_at)), 1) AS avg_days_early
FROM orders
WHERE delivered_at IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY state
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 500
ORDER BY pct_late DESC
LIMIT 12;

title: Which states hold most of the late orders?
why: Late rate tells you where it is bad. Volume tells you where fixing it matters.
sql:
SELECT state,
       SUM(delivered_at > estimated_at) AS late_orders,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(delivered_at > estimated_at)
             / (SELECT SUM(delivered_at > estimated_at) FROM orders WHERE delivered_at IS NOT NULL), 1) AS pct_of_late,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE delivered_at IS NOT NULL), 1) AS pct_of_orders
FROM orders
WHERE delivered_at IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY state
ORDER BY late_orders DESC
LIMIT 8;

title: Is lateness spread out, or concentrated in a few sellers?
why: Sellers ranked by late orders. How much of all lateness comes from the worst 5% of sellers?
sql:
WITH so AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT i.seller_id, o.order_id,
         o.delivered_at > o.estimated_at AS late
  FROM orders o JOIN items i USING (order_id)
  WHERE o.delivered_at IS NOT NULL
), s AS (
  SELECT seller_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(late) AS late
  FROM so GROUP BY seller_id
), ranked AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY late DESC) AS rk,
         COUNT(*) OVER () AS n
  FROM s
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS worst_sellers,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(late) / (SELECT SUM(late) FROM s), 1) AS pct_of_late_orders,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(orders) / (SELECT SUM(orders) FROM s), 1) AS pct_of_all_orders
FROM ranked
WHERE rk <= n * 0.05;

title: Do orders split across sellers fare worse?
why: Orders with items from more than one seller arrive in several parcels.
sql:
WITH s AS (
  SELECT order_id, COUNT(DISTINCT seller_id) AS n
  FROM items GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT CASE WHEN n = 1 THEN 'One seller' ELSE 'Two or more' END AS sellers_in_order,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       ROUND(AVG(r.score), 2) AS avg_score,
       ROUND(100.0 * AVG(r.score <= 2), 1) AS pct_bad
FROM s JOIN reviews r USING (order_id)
GROUP BY sellers_in_order;

title: What is the most that fixing lateness could gain?
why: An upper bound: if every late order had been rated like an on-time order. It assumes nothing else about those orders differs, so it is an estimate, not a forecast.
sql:
WITH d AS (
  SELECT CASE
           WHEN o.delivered_at IS NULL THEN 'Not delivered'
           WHEN o.delivered_at > o.estimated_at THEN 'Late'
           ELSE 'On time'
         END AS delivery, r.score
  FROM orders o JOIN reviews r USING (order_id)
), ot AS (
  SELECT AVG(score) AS s, AVG(score <= 2) AS b FROM d WHERE delivery = 'On time'
)
SELECT ROUND(AVG(score), 2) AS avg_score_now,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN delivery = 'Late' THEN (SELECT s FROM ot) ELSE score END), 2) AS avg_score_if_on_time,
       SUM(score <= 2) AS bad_reviews_now,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN delivery = 'Late' THEN (SELECT b FROM ot) ELSE score <= 2 END)) AS bad_reviews_if_on_time
FROM d;
